poolName: Messaging & Integration: SNS, SQS, Amazon MQ, MSK & AppFlow (Mixed Difficulty)
description: SAA-C03 revision questions on Amazon SNS, Amazon SQS, Amazon MQ, Amazon MSK and Amazon AppFlow at Easy, Medium and Hard difficulty: decoupling, fanout, ordering and delivery guarantees, filtering, visibility and polling, protocols, streaming and SaaS data integration.

questions.prompt: A marketing team wants to copy data from a SaaS application into Amazon S3 on a regular basis without writing or maintaining integration code. Which service is designed for this?
choices: Amazon SQS
Amazon AppFlow
Amazon MSK
Amazon MQ
questions.correctChoice: Amazon AppFlow
questions.explanation: AppFlow is a managed integration service that transfers data between SaaS applications and AWS services such as S3 through configured flows, with no custom code needed.

questions.prompt: Which set lists the ways an Amazon AppFlow flow can be triggered?
choices: On a schedule or by an SQS queue message, but never on demand
Only on demand, started manually by an administrator in the console
On demand, on a schedule, or on an event from a SaaS application
Only on a recurring schedule that is defined with a cron expression
questions.correctChoice: On demand, on a schedule, or on an event from a SaaS application
questions.explanation: AppFlow flows can be run manually (on demand), on a recurring schedule, or on an event from a supported SaaS application.

questions.prompt: A company wants customer data copied to AWS immediately whenever a record changes in its SaaS CRM, rather than waiting for a nightly job. Which AppFlow configuration fits best?
choices: A flow that runs on an event from the SaaS application
A flow that runs on a schedule every 24 hours
A flow that runs on demand each morning
A flow that runs only when an administrator chooses to start it
questions.correctChoice: A flow that runs on an event from the SaaS application
questions.explanation: Event-triggered flows run in response to an event in the SaaS application, giving near-real-time transfer. Scheduled and on-demand flows are not driven by data changes.

questions.prompt: Security policy forbids sending SaaS data over the public internet. A team still wants to move data from a supported SaaS application into AWS using AppFlow. Which feature helps?
choices: Flows that disable encryption to reduce latency
Flows that use a Lambda function to open a public endpoint
Flows that run on a schedule only
Private flows that use AWS PrivateLink
questions.correctChoice: Private flows that use AWS PrivateLink
questions.explanation: AppFlow can create private flows over AWS PrivateLink so that data stays on the AWS network rather than crossing the public internet. Data can also be encrypted in transit and at rest.

questions.prompt: A company ingests SaaS data into S3 with AppFlow and wants analysts to query it with SQL-based tools without hand-defining table schemas. What should be configured?
choices: Use Amazon MQ to hold the schema definitions
Catalogue the transferred data in the AWS Glue Data Catalog from the flow settings
Attach an SQS queue to the S3 bucket and read the table definitions from messages
Send the data through an SNS topic with a filter policy
questions.correctChoice: Catalogue the transferred data in the AWS Glue Data Catalog from the flow settings
questions.explanation: AppFlow can register data it writes to S3 in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, making it discoverable for query services. Partition and aggregation settings can also improve query performance.

questions.prompt: A team needs a scheduled, encrypted transfer of SaaS records to S3, with partitioning and aggregation applied, and wants the least operational overhead. Which option is best?
choices: Run Apache Kafka on EC2 and build a connector for the SaaS application
Write a Lambda function with scheduled invocations and custom API logic for the SaaS application
Configure an AppFlow flow with a schedule trigger and the partition and aggregation settings
Run a custom polling application on EC2 with an SQS queue buffering the records
questions.correctChoice: Configure an AppFlow flow with a schedule trigger and the partition and aggregation settings
questions.explanation: AppFlow provides scheduled flows, encryption, and partition and aggregation options as managed features. The alternatives all require building and operating custom integration code or infrastructure.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of Amazon SNS in an architecture?
choices: Streaming ordered logs in partitions so consumers can replay them
Running containerised workloads without managing the servers
Holding messages in a queue until one consumer polls for them
Pub/sub messaging that decouples publishers from subscribers
questions.correctChoice: Pub/sub messaging that decouples publishers from subscribers
questions.explanation: SNS is a fully managed publish/subscribe service. Publishers send to a topic and SNS pushes copies to all subscribers, so publishers need not know who receives the messages.

questions.prompt: In Amazon SNS, what is a topic?
choices: A logical channel that publishers send to and subscribers attach to
A rule that filters messages according to their attribute values
A Kafka partition that stores streaming records in order
A queue from which consumers poll for their messages in batches
questions.correctChoice: A logical channel that publishers send to and subscribers attach to
questions.explanation: The SNS topic acts as the event bus: publishers send to it, and each subscription on the topic receives the messages. Publishers need not care about the subscribers' protocols.

questions.prompt: Which of these SNS subscriber types is classed as application-to-person (A2P) rather than application-to-application (A2A)?
choices: An AWS Lambda function that is triggered by the topic
An HTTPS endpoint that is registered as a webhook
An SMS text message sent to a mobile phone number
An SQS queue that receives the messages
questions.correctChoice: An SMS text message sent to a mobile phone number
questions.explanation: A2P destinations deliver to people: SMS, email and mobile push. A2A destinations include SQS, Lambda, Firehose and HTTP/S endpoints.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts SNS standard topics with SNS FIFO topics?
choices: FIFO topics preserve message order and deduplicate, with lower throughput than standard topics
Standard topics have lower throughput than FIFO topics
FIFO topics deliver at least once and may duplicate, whereas standard topics never duplicate
Standard topics preserve strict order, whereas FIFO topics do not
questions.correctChoice: FIFO topics preserve message order and deduplicate, with lower throughput than standard topics
questions.explanation: Standard topics offer very high throughput with at-least-once delivery and no guaranteed order. FIFO topics guarantee ordering within a message group and deduplicate, at lower throughput.

questions.prompt: A developer creates an SNS FIFO topic. Which requirement applies to the topic name?
choices: It must include the Region code
It must be exactly 10 characters long
It must begin with the prefix fifo-
It must end with the .fifo suffix
questions.correctChoice: It must end with the .fifo suffix
questions.explanation: FIFO topics (and FIFO queues) must have names ending in .fifo, and the topic is created with the FifoTopic attribute set to true.

questions.prompt: A Lambda function subscribed to a standard SNS topic occasionally processes the same notification twice. What is the best way to keep the results correct?
choices: Move the Lambda subscription into a different Availability Zone
Make processing idempotent, because standard topics deliver at least once
Enable raw message delivery on the Lambda subscription to the topic
Raise the topic's throughput limit so that duplicates stop occurring
questions.correctChoice: Make processing idempotent, because standard topics deliver at least once
questions.explanation: Standard SNS topics guarantee at-least-once delivery, so duplicates are possible. Idempotent consumers handle them safely; otherwise use a FIFO topic with deduplication.

questions.prompt: An order service must send each new order to three independent systems (billing, inventory, shipping). Each system processes at its own pace and must not lose orders if it is temporarily down. Which design fits best?
choices: Publish to one shared SQS queue that all three systems poll
Publish to an SNS topic with the three systems subscribed by email
Have the order service call each of the systems directly over HTTP
Publish to an SNS topic with one subscribed SQS queue per system
questions.correctChoice: Publish to an SNS topic with one subscribed SQS queue per system
questions.explanation: The SNS-to-SQS fanout pattern gives each consumer its own durable buffer. With a single shared queue, each message would go to only one consumer.

questions.prompt: Only one of five subscribers on an SNS topic wants messages where the attribute eventType equals "refund". How can this be achieved without changing the publisher?
choices: Attach a dead-letter queue to the topic itself
Enable raw message delivery on that one subscriber
Apply a subscription filter policy to that one subscriber
Create five separate topics and make the publisher send to each
questions.correctChoice: Apply a subscription filter policy to that one subscriber
questions.explanation: Filter policies are applied per subscription, so SNS delivers only matching messages to that subscriber. The publisher still publishes once.

questions.prompt: Messages published to an SNS topic carry the values to filter on inside the JSON message body, not in message attributes. Which setting lets a subscription filter policy match on them?
choices: Set the filter policy scope to MessageBody
Set the filter policy scope to MessageAttributes
Enable FIFO on the topic
Enable server-side encryption on the topic
questions.correctChoice: Set the filter policy scope to MessageBody
questions.explanation: A filter policy applies to message attributes by default (MessageAttributes scope). Setting the scope to MessageBody lets it match on fields in the payload.

questions.prompt: A subscription should receive only order messages whose numeric attribute price is greater than 100. Which type of filter policy matching supports this?
choices: Prefix matching on a string value
Numeric range matching
IP address matching
Case-insensitive string matching
questions.correctChoice: Numeric range matching
questions.explanation: Filter policies support numeric matching, including exact, anything-but and range comparisons. String matching options such as prefix operate on text rather than on numbers.

questions.prompt: An SQS queue subscribed to an SNS topic receives the message wrapped in an SNS JSON envelope, and the consumer wants only the original payload. What should be enabled?
choices: A larger visibility timeout on the queue
A FIFO topic instead of a standard topic
Long polling on the receiving queue
Raw message delivery on the subscription
questions.correctChoice: Raw message delivery on the subscription
questions.explanation: With raw message delivery enabled for SQS, Firehose or HTTP/S subscriptions, SNS sends the message as-is without the JSON envelope, which avoids parsing and reduces payload size.

questions.prompt: A team wants undeliverable messages from an SNS subscription kept in a dead-letter queue. The subscribed endpoint is a standard SQS queue. Which dead-letter queue configuration is valid?
choices: A FIFO SQS queue, because dead-letter queues must always be FIFO
A standard SQS queue whose access policy lets SNS send messages to it
A second SNS topic that is subscribed to the first one
A Kinesis data stream that is attached to the subscription
questions.correctChoice: A standard SQS queue whose access policy lets SNS send messages to it
questions.explanation: The SNS DLQ must be an SQS queue of the same type as the topic (standard for standard, FIFO for FIFO), and its queue policy must permit SNS to send to it.

questions.prompt: An SNS topic delivers to an HTTPS webhook that is sometimes down for extended periods. Operations must be able to inspect and replay the messages SNS could not deliver, with little custom code. What should they do?
choices: Enable Message Data Protection on the topic
Switch the topic to FIFO so that retries are unlimited
Attach an SQS dead-letter queue to the subscription
Increase the topic's maximum message size
questions.correctChoice: Attach an SQS dead-letter queue to the subscription
questions.explanation: After the delivery policy's retries are exhausted, SNS can move undeliverable messages into an SQS DLQ attached to the subscription, where they can be inspected and reprocessed.

questions.prompt: A trading app must send each customer's transactions to several downstream systems in the exact order they were created, with no duplicates, and each system must process at its own pace. Which design meets this?
choices: An SNS FIFO topic with SQS FIFO queues, using customer ID as the message group ID
A standard SNS topic with Lambda subscribers and a DynamoDB table for deduplication
An SNS FIFO topic with email subscriptions for each downstream team
A standard SNS topic with SQS standard queues, relying on timestamps for order
questions.correctChoice: An SNS FIFO topic with SQS FIFO queues, using customer ID as the message group ID
questions.explanation: FIFO topics preserve order within a message group and deduplicate, and SQS FIFO subscribers let each system consume at its own pace. Standard topics give no ordering guarantee.

questions.prompt: A publisher retries a publish to an SNS FIFO topic after a timeout, sending the same message with the same deduplication ID about 2 minutes after the first attempt. What happens?
choices: SNS rejects the publish with an error and stops the topic
SNS treats it as a duplicate and does not deliver it a second time
SNS delivers it twice, because FIFO topics never deduplicate
SNS delivers it twice, but marks the second copy as a duplicate
questions.correctChoice: SNS treats it as a duplicate and does not deliver it a second time
questions.explanation: FIFO topics deduplicate messages, using a deduplication ID or content-based deduplication, within a 5-minute interval, so the retry is not delivered again.

questions.prompt: An e-commerce platform publishes all order events to one SNS topic with a message attribute orderType (standard, express, international). Three fulfilment SQS queues should each receive only their own order type, and new order types must be added without changing the publisher. What is the best design?
choices: Three separate topics, with the publisher deciding which one to use
One SQS queue with three consumers that skip the wrong order types
One topic with a filter policy on each queue's subscription matching its orderType
One topic where each consumer discards messages that are not theirs after receiving
questions.correctChoice: One topic with a filter policy on each queue's subscription matching its orderType
questions.explanation: Subscription filter policies let SNS route messages based on attributes, keeping the publisher simple and unaware of consumers. Discarding after receipt wastes processing and queue capacity.

questions.prompt: A subscriber should receive every message published to an SNS topic except those whose attribute env equals "test". Which filter policy matching type supports this?
choices: Anything-but matching on the env attribute
IP address matching on the env attribute using the value test
Numeric range matching on the env attribute using the value test
Prefix matching on the env attribute set to the value test
questions.correctChoice: Anything-but matching on the env attribute
questions.explanation: Filter policies support anything-but matching for numeric and string values, which delivers all messages except those matching the listed values. Prefix, range and IP address matching select matches rather than excluding them.

questions.prompt: A company must archive every message published to an SNS topic into S3 for audit, and must also trigger a Lambda function for each message, with no custom archiving code. Which design fits best?
choices: Subscribe an email address and forward the messages from the mailbox into S3
Subscribe an HTTP endpoint that stores each message in S3 using a script running on EC2
Subscribe only the Lambda function and have it write each message to an SQS queue for archiving
Subscribe both an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream to S3 and the Lambda function to the topic
questions.correctChoice: Subscribe both an Amazon Data Firehose delivery stream to S3 and the Lambda function to the topic
questions.explanation: Firehose is a supported SNS subscriber that can deliver messages to S3, and the same topic can also invoke Lambda, since one published message reaches all subscriptions. The other options need custom code or manual steps.

questions.prompt: How can the messages stored in an SNS topic be encrypted at rest?
choices: Enable long polling on the topic with a 20-second wait time
Apply a filter policy to every subscription on the topic
Add a .fifo suffix to the topic name to switch on encryption
Enable server-side encryption on the topic with an AWS KMS key
questions.correctChoice: Enable server-side encryption on the topic with an AWS KMS key
questions.explanation: SNS topics support server-side encryption with AWS KMS keys. Filter policies, long polling and FIFO have nothing to do with encryption.

questions.prompt: A publisher must send payloads of several hundred megabytes through SNS, well beyond the maximum message size. What is the supported approach?
choices: Raise the SNS message size limit to 2 GB in the topic settings
Compress the payload and then enable raw message delivery
Use the SNS Extended Client Library, which stores the payload in S3
Split the payload across messages by using a FIFO topic
questions.correctChoice: Use the SNS Extended Client Library, which stores the payload in S3
questions.explanation: The Extended Client Library uses S3 to hold large payloads (up to 2 GB) and publishes a pointer. The plain message size limit is far smaller and cannot be raised to 2 GB.

questions.prompt: Which SNS subscription protocol delivers push notifications to apps installed on mobile devices?
choices: HTTP/S
Platform application endpoint
Email-JSON
Amazon SQS
questions.correctChoice: Platform application endpoint
questions.explanation: Mobile push uses the platform application endpoint protocol. Email, SMS and HTTP/S deliver through other channels.

questions.prompt: Which SNS subscriber type allows its delivery retry policy, including the backoff function, to be customised?
choices: HTTP/S endpoints
Amazon Data Firehose streams
SQS queues
AWS Lambda functions
questions.correctChoice: HTTP/S endpoints
questions.explanation: Delivery policies for SQS, Lambda and Firehose are fixed by SNS, whereas HTTP/S endpoints can use a custom policy, including linear, arithmetic, geometric or exponential backoff.

questions.prompt: An operations mailbox must receive alerts from two different SNS topics. How must this be set up?
choices: Create one email subscription and use a filter policy to add the second topic
Create a separate email subscription on each topic
Create one email subscription that is attached to both topics
Create one topic subscription and attach the second topic to it
questions.correctChoice: Create a separate email subscription on each topic
questions.explanation: A subscription belongs to exactly one topic and uses exactly one protocol, so receiving from two topics needs two subscriptions.

questions.prompt: A publisher sends many small messages to SNS and wants to reduce API request costs. What can it do?
choices: Batch publishing, sending up to 10 messages per request
Using short polling on the topic itself
Publishing every message twice so that one copy succeeds
Using long polling on the publisher's side
questions.correctChoice: Batch publishing, sending up to 10 messages per request
questions.explanation: SNS supports batching up to 10 messages per publish request, which lowers the number of API requests and therefore the cost.

questions.prompt: A web tier accepts uploads and a separate worker tier processes them. Traffic is spiky, and the web tier must not be slowed down or fail when workers are busy. Which service best decouples the two tiers?
choices: AWS Service Catalog
Amazon Cognito
Amazon SQS
AWS Certificate Manager
questions.correctChoice: Amazon SQS
questions.explanation: SQS provides asynchronous communication between producers and consumers. Messages wait safely in the queue until workers are ready, absorbing traffic spikes.

questions.prompt: How do consumers receive messages from an Amazon SQS queue?
choices: SQS invokes the consumers through an HTTP webhook
SQS broadcasts each message to all consumers at once
SQS pushes messages to consumers in real time
They poll the queue to pull messages
questions.correctChoice: They poll the queue to pull messages
questions.explanation: SQS is pull-based: consumers must poll. SNS is the service that pushes messages to its subscribers.

questions.prompt: Which statement about SQS standard queues versus FIFO queues is correct?
choices: Standard queues guarantee strict ordering, but FIFO queues do not guarantee ordering
Standard queues have nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering
FIFO queues have unlimited throughput by default, but standard queues are limited to 300 per second
Standard queues guarantee exactly-once processing, but FIFO queues may deliver duplicates
questions.correctChoice: Standard queues have nearly unlimited throughput, at-least-once delivery and best-effort ordering
questions.explanation: Standard queues maximise throughput but can deliver duplicates and out-of-order messages. FIFO queues preserve order and avoid duplicates, with lower throughput.

questions.prompt: A message in a standard SQS queue has not been consumed after 4 days, and the retention period was never changed. What happens to the message?
choices: It is deleted, because the default retention period is 4 days
It is deleted after 30 seconds, the default visibility timeout
It is moved to a dead-letter queue automatically
It stays until a consumer processes it, because queues store messages indefinitely
questions.correctChoice: It is deleted, because the default retention period is 4 days
questions.explanation: Retention defaults to 4 days and can be set from 60 seconds to 14 days. After that, SQS deletes the message.

questions.prompt: What does the SQS visibility timeout do?
choices: It defines how long the messages are stored before they are deleted
It sets how long a consumer waits for new messages to arrive in the queue
It delays a newly sent message from appearing in the queue at all
It hides a message from other consumers for a time after one receives it
questions.correctChoice: It hides a message from other consumers for a time after one receives it
questions.explanation: After a consumer receives a message, it is invisible to others for the visibility timeout so it is not processed twice. If it is not deleted in time, it becomes visible again.

questions.prompt: A consumer receives a message from an SQS queue and finishes processing it. What must the consumer do next?
choices: Re-send the message with a new ID
Wait for the retention period to expire
Delete the message from the queue
Nothing, because SQS removes a message when it is read
questions.correctChoice: Delete the message from the queue
questions.explanation: Receiving a message does not remove it. The consumer must explicitly delete it; otherwise it reappears after the visibility timeout and is processed again.

questions.prompt: Each message takes about 90 seconds to process, but some messages are being processed twice by different workers. The queue uses the default settings. What is the most likely cause and fix?
choices: Short polling is the cause, so the queue should be switched to FIFO
The retention period is too long, so it should be reduced to 60 seconds
The queue's delay is too short, so DelaySeconds should be raised above 90
The 30-second visibility timeout is too short; raise it above 90 seconds
questions.correctChoice: The 30-second visibility timeout is too short; raise it above 90 seconds
questions.explanation: If a message is not deleted before the visibility timeout (default 30 seconds) ends, it becomes visible again and another worker takes it. Setting the timeout above the processing time prevents this.

questions.prompt: A worker receives a message and then crashes before finishing. What happens to that message?
choices: It is deleted automatically as soon as the first worker has received it
It stays hidden from all consumers until the queue's retention period ends
It becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and another worker takes it
It is lost permanently, because it was already received one time before
questions.correctChoice: It becomes visible again after the visibility timeout and another worker takes it
questions.explanation: Because the message was never deleted, it becomes visible again after the visibility timeout expires, which is what makes SQS processing resilient to worker failures.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum value that can be set for an SQS queue's visibility timeout?
choices: 24 hours
12 hours
15 minutes
14 days
questions.correctChoice: 12 hours
questions.explanation: Visibility timeout ranges from 0 seconds to 12 hours (default 30 seconds). Fifteen minutes is the maximum delay queue setting and 14 days is the maximum retention.

questions.prompt: A worker fleet polls an SQS queue that is empty most of the day, and the bill shows a very high number of empty receives. What is the simplest fix?
choices: Enable long polling so that receive calls wait for messages to arrive
Reduce the retention period of the queue to a few minutes
Switch the queue to a FIFO queue with the .fifo suffix
Increase the delay of the queue to the maximum of 15 minutes
questions.correctChoice: Enable long polling so that receive calls wait for messages to arrive
questions.explanation: Short polling (the default) returns immediately even when empty, creating many billable empty responses. Long polling waits (up to 20 seconds) for messages, reducing empty receives and cost.

questions.prompt: Which statement about SQS short polling and long polling is correct?
choices: Long polling returns at once even if the queue is empty, while short polling waits for a message
Long polling is available only on standard queues, while short polling is available on all queues
Short polling is available only on FIFO queues, while long polling is available on all queues
Short polling returns at once even if the queue is empty, while long polling waits for a message or the timeout
questions.correctChoice: Short polling returns at once even if the queue is empty, while long polling waits for a message or the timeout
questions.explanation: Short polling is the default and returns immediately. Long polling waits until a message arrives or the wait time ends, which lowers cost by reducing empty receives.

questions.prompt: A producer sends messages that consumers should not see for the first 5 minutes after they are sent. Which SQS feature applies to all messages in the queue?
choices: Long polling with a wait time of 5 minutes
A delay queue with DelaySeconds set to 300
A retention period of 5 minutes on the queue
A visibility timeout of 300 seconds on the queue
questions.correctChoice: A delay queue with DelaySeconds set to 300
questions.explanation: A delay queue keeps newly added messages invisible for the configured delay (up to 15 minutes). Visibility timeout, by contrast, applies after a message has been received.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes a delay queue from the visibility timeout?
choices: A delay hides a message when it is first added, whereas the visibility timeout hides it after it is consumed
Both hide messages only after they are consumed, but for different lengths of time
A delay hides a message after it is consumed, whereas the visibility timeout hides it when first added
Both hide messages when first added, but one is set per message
questions.correctChoice: A delay hides a message when it is first added, whereas the visibility timeout hides it after it is consumed
questions.explanation: DelaySeconds postpones when a new message first becomes available, while the visibility timeout hides a message that a consumer has already received.

questions.prompt: Most messages in a standard queue should be available immediately, but one message type should become visible only after 10 minutes. Which feature is best?
choices: A visibility timeout of 600 seconds on the queue
A queue-level delay of 600 seconds that applies to every message
A message timer that sets DelaySeconds on just those messages
A retention period of 10 minutes on the whole queue
questions.correctChoice: A message timer that sets DelaySeconds on just those messages
questions.explanation: Message timers set an initial invisibility period per message using DelaySeconds at the message level. A queue-level delay would delay every message.

questions.prompt: Most messages in a queue take 20 seconds to process, but a few take up to 10 minutes. A global 10-minute visibility timeout would delay retries of failed ordinary messages. What is a better approach?
choices: Set the retention period to 10 minutes so that slow messages are never lost
Convert the queue to FIFO so that slow messages are processed more quickly
Keep a short timeout and have consumers extend the visibility of long-running messages while working
Turn on long polling so slow messages are held by the consumer
questions.correctChoice: Keep a short timeout and have consumers extend the visibility of long-running messages while working
questions.explanation: A consumer can extend the visibility timeout of an individual message it is still processing (ChangeMessageVisibility), so retries of failed ordinary messages stay quick while slow messages are not picked up by another worker.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the message group ID in an SQS FIFO queue?
choices: It determines how long the messages in that group are kept in the queue
Messages in a group stay in order, and different groups can be consumed in parallel
It makes the queue use a separate encryption key for every group of messages
It identifies the one consumer that is the only one allowed to read each message
questions.correctChoice: Messages in a group stay in order, and different groups can be consumed in parallel
questions.explanation: FIFO ordering is preserved per message group, which allows multiple ordered streams within one queue and parallel consumption across groups.

questions.prompt: A FIFO queue must keep each customer's events in order, but a single consumer is too slow for overall volume. Which design scales consumption while preserving per-customer order?
choices: Use one constant message group ID for all messages and run multiple consumers
Use a message timer on each message to stagger processing
Switch to a standard queue and run multiple consumers
Use the customer ID as the message group ID and run multiple consumers
questions.correctChoice: Use the customer ID as the message group ID and run multiple consumers
questions.explanation: Ordering applies within a message group, so grouping by customer lets consumers process different customers in parallel. A single group ID would serialise everything.

questions.prompt: A team realises an existing standard queue needs strict ordering. What must they do?
choices: Create a new FIFO queue and move the producers and consumers over to it
Enable long polling on the existing queue so that its messages are ordered
Edit the existing queue's attributes so that its type is changed to FIFO
Add a .fifo suffix to the name of the existing standard queue
questions.correctChoice: Create a new FIFO queue and move the producers and consumers over to it
questions.explanation: A queue's type cannot be converted. A new FIFO queue (with a name ending in .fifo) must be created and the applications pointed to it.

questions.prompt: A FIFO queue handling order events is limiting throughput as volume grows. Ordering and no duplicates must be kept. Which option should be tried first?
choices: Use batching and turn on high throughput mode for the FIFO queue
Switch every one of the consumers over to short polling
Convert the queue into a standard queue to remove its limits
Raise the visibility timeout on the queue up to the 12-hour maximum
questions.correctChoice: Use batching and turn on high throughput mode for the FIFO queue
questions.explanation: FIFO queues have lower throughput than standard queues, but batching (up to 10 messages per request) and high throughput mode raise the limits while retaining ordering and deduplication.

questions.prompt: A payment system must process transactions for each account strictly in the order submitted and must never apply a transaction twice. Peak volume is moderate. Which option is best?
choices: An SQS standard queue with a 12-hour visibility timeout
An SQS standard queue, because order is usually preserved
An SQS FIFO queue with message group IDs based on the account
An SNS standard topic, because it guarantees delivery order
questions.correctChoice: An SQS FIFO queue with message group IDs based on the account
questions.explanation: FIFO queues guarantee ordering within a group and avoid duplicates. Standard queues only give best-effort ordering and can deliver duplicates; a longer visibility timeout does not provide ordering.

questions.prompt: A producer must send messages up to 1 GB through SQS. How can this be done?
choices: Enable long polling so that large messages are accepted
Raise the queue's maximum message size to 2 GB
Switch to a FIFO queue, which has no limit on message size
Use the SQS Extended Client Library, which keeps the payload in S3
questions.correctChoice: Use the SQS Extended Client Library, which keeps the payload in S3
questions.explanation: The Extended Client Library stores the payload in an S3 bucket and places a pointer in the queue, supporting payloads up to 2 GB. The built-in message size limit is far smaller.

questions.prompt: A compliance team requires that messages at rest in an SQS queue be encrypted with a key whose usage can be audited and controlled by the company. What should be configured?
choices: A FIFO queue that uses content-based deduplication
Server-side encryption with a customer managed KMS key
A message timer applied to every message in the queue
Long polling configured with a custom wait time
questions.correctChoice: Server-side encryption with a customer managed KMS key
questions.explanation: SQS supports server-side encryption using SQS-managed keys or AWS KMS keys. A customer managed KMS key gives control over the key policy and auditable key usage through CloudTrail.

questions.prompt: An SNS topic is subscribed to an SQS queue in the same account, but messages never arrive. Subscription settings look correct. What is the most likely missing piece?
choices: The queue's access policy does not allow the SNS topic to send messages
The queue needs a longer retention period so messages can arrive
The topic needs a visibility timeout configured
The queue needs to be converted to a FIFO queue
questions.correctChoice: The queue's access policy does not allow the SNS topic to send messages
questions.explanation: SQS access policies are resource-based policies. The queue must grant sqs:SendMessage to the topic (for example, with the topic ARN as a condition) before SNS can deliver messages to it.

questions.prompt: Which set contains condition keys that SQS attribute-based access control (ABAC) uses to control access based on tags?
choices: kms:ViaService, kms:CallerAccount and kms:KeySpec
sqs:VisibilityTimeout, sqs:DelaySeconds and sqs:MessageGroupId
aws:ResourceTag, aws:RequestTag and aws:TagKeys
aws:SourceIp, aws:UserAgent and aws:MultiFactorAuthAge
questions.correctChoice: aws:ResourceTag, aws:RequestTag and aws:TagKeys
questions.explanation: ABAC authorises actions using tags on users and resources, with the global condition keys aws:ResourceTag, aws:RequestTag and aws:TagKeys.

questions.prompt: A company tags queues with environment=prod or environment=dev. Developers' IAM roles must not send, receive or delete messages on queues tagged prod, even if other policies allow it, and the rule must apply to queues created in future. What is the best approach?
choices: FIFO turned on for every one of the queues that are tagged prod
An Allow statement that names each of the existing dev queues individually
A very short visibility timeout that is set on every queue tagged prod
A Deny on the SQS actions, conditioned on aws:ResourceTag/environment being prod
questions.correctChoice: A Deny on the SQS actions, conditioned on aws:ResourceTag/environment being prod
questions.explanation: A tag-based Deny using aws:ResourceTag applies automatically to any queue with that tag, and an explicit Deny overrides any Allow. Naming each queue does not cover future ones.

questions.prompt: A request-response pattern needs lightweight per-client reply queues that are created and removed constantly, at minimal cost. Which SQS feature fits?
choices: Delay queues that are configured with a 15-minute delay
Temporary queues created with the Temporary Queue Client
Queues that use message timers on each reply
FIFO queues that are polled using long polling
questions.correctChoice: Temporary queues created with the Temporary Queue Client
questions.explanation: The Temporary Queue Client creates lightweight, application-managed queues that are removed automatically when no longer in use, with no extra cost for creating and deleting them.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum number of messages that can be sent in a single SQS batch request?
questions.explanation: SQS batch actions handle up to 10 messages per request, which can reduce cost and increase throughput.

questions.prompt: Worker instances in an Auto Scaling group process jobs from an SQS queue. Queue backlog varies widely, and CPU utilisation is a poor indicator of load. Which scaling approach is best?
choices: Scale on the network out metric that is reported by the instances
Scale on a fixed schedule that adds capacity at the start of each hour
Scale on the retention period that is configured on the queue itself
Scale on backlog per instance, based on the number of visible messages
questions.correctChoice: Scale on backlog per instance, based on the number of visible messages
questions.explanation: Queue depth reflects the actual work waiting, so a target-tracking policy on backlog per instance scales workers up and down with demand, and SQS buffers work in the meantime.

questions.prompt: A few malformed messages cause consumers to fail repeatedly, and the messages keep reappearing and blocking worker capacity. What is the best way to isolate them for investigation?
choices: Reduce the retention period of the queue down to 60 seconds
Add a dead-letter queue with a maximum receive count to the source queue
Raise the visibility timeout to 12 hours for all of the messages in it
Convert the source queue into a FIFO queue to block the bad messages
questions.correctChoice: Add a dead-letter queue with a maximum receive count to the source queue
questions.explanation: A dead-letter queue with a maxReceiveCount moves messages that fail repeatedly into a separate queue for analysis, instead of cycling endlessly in the source queue.

questions.prompt: A team wants to attach structured metadata, such as a numeric priority and a binary image type, to SQS messages without changing the message body. What should they use?
choices: Message attributes, with types such as String, Number and Binary
Queue tags that are set on the queue by the administrator
The visibility timeout setting that is configured on the queue
The access policy that is attached to the queue as a resource policy
questions.correctChoice: Message attributes, with types such as String, Number and Binary
questions.explanation: Message attributes carry structured metadata with the message. Types include String, Number and Binary, and a custom label can be appended (for example, Number.byte).

questions.prompt: A Lambda function with a 5-minute timeout consumes an SQS queue that has the default 30-second visibility timeout. Messages are being processed more than once. What should be changed?
choices: Set the queue's visibility timeout to at least the function's timeout
Reduce the function's timeout to 1 second so that it fails faster
Set the queue's retention period to only 60 seconds so old messages vanish
Enable raw message delivery on the queue so messages are not retried
questions.correctChoice: Set the queue's visibility timeout to at least the function's timeout
questions.explanation: If the visibility timeout is shorter than the processing time, messages become visible again while still being processed and get retried. The visibility timeout should be at least as long as the function timeout.

questions.prompt: A producer accidentally sends the same order twice within a minute to a FIFO queue using the same deduplication ID. How many copies will consumers receive?
choices: Zero, because duplicates are rejected and then removed along with the original
One, as FIFO queues deduplicate within a 5-minute interval
Two, because every send is stored by the queue as a separate message
Two, but the second one is flagged as a duplicate for the consumers
questions.correctChoice: One, as FIFO queues deduplicate within a 5-minute interval
questions.explanation: FIFO queues use the message deduplication ID (or content-based deduplication) to discard duplicates sent within a 5-minute interval.

questions.prompt: A photo app queues thumbnail jobs. Volume is very high, jobs are independent and order does not matter, and an occasional repeated job is harmless. Which queue type is the best fit?
choices: A FIFO queue with a message timer
A temporary queue with a FIFO suffix
A standard queue
A FIFO queue with one message group
questions.correctChoice: A standard queue
questions.explanation: Standard queues offer nearly unlimited throughput and are best when order and exactly-once delivery are not crucial. FIFO adds throughput limits that are not needed here.

questions.prompt: Four microservices must each process every message produced by a single publisher. A team puts one SQS queue between the publisher and the four services, and finds each message is handled by only one service. What should they change?
choices: Increase the retention period so each service gets a turn
Convert the queue to FIFO so that every service receives each message
Raise the visibility timeout so all four services can read each message
Publish to an SNS topic and give each service its own subscribed SQS queue
questions.correctChoice: Publish to an SNS topic and give each service its own subscribed SQS queue
questions.explanation: Consumers sharing one queue compete for messages. Fanning out through an SNS topic into one queue per service gives each service its own copy of every message.

questions.prompt: A company has an on-premises application that uses Apache ActiveMQ and the JMS API. It wants to move to AWS with as few code changes as possible. Which service fits best?
choices: Amazon SNS
Amazon SQS
Amazon MQ
Amazon AppFlow
questions.correctChoice: Amazon MQ
questions.explanation: Amazon MQ is a managed broker for Apache ActiveMQ and RabbitMQ that supports industry-standard APIs and protocols, so existing applications can migrate without being rewritten for SQS or SNS APIs.

questions.prompt: A new cloud-native application needs simple, highly scalable queue-based decoupling, with no dependence on existing broker protocols. Which choice is the most appropriate and the least to operate?
choices: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
Amazon SQS
A self-managed RabbitMQ cluster on EC2
Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ
questions.correctChoice: Amazon SQS
questions.explanation: For new applications without protocol requirements, SQS is serverless and scales automatically. Amazon MQ is mainly for migrating applications that rely on standard broker protocols or advanced messaging features.

questions.prompt: A fleet of devices publishes telemetry to a broker using MQTT. Which AWS messaging service supports MQTT brokers for applications that need standard messaging protocols?
choices: Amazon SQS
Amazon SNS standard topics
AWS AppFlow
Amazon MQ
questions.correctChoice: Amazon MQ
questions.explanation: Amazon MQ supports standard protocols such as AMQP, MQTT and STOMP (and OpenWire for ActiveMQ). SQS and SNS use AWS APIs rather than these broker protocols.

questions.prompt: In AMQP messaging on a broker such as RabbitMQ, how do messages get from publishers to queues?
choices: Publishers send to exchanges, which route copies to queues using bindings
Publishers send straight to consumers, bypassing the broker
Publishers write to a shared database that consumers query
Publishers send to SNS topics, which forward the messages to queues
questions.correctChoice: Publishers send to exchanges, which route copies to queues using bindings
questions.explanation: AMQP publishers publish to exchanges, and exchanges distribute message copies to queues using rules called bindings. Consumers then receive from the queues.

questions.prompt: In AMQP, when is a message removed from a queue?
choices: When the publisher sends the next message
When the visibility timeout expires
As soon as the broker delivers it
When a consumer acknowledges it to the broker
questions.correctChoice: When a consumer acknowledges it to the broker
questions.explanation: A message stays in the queue until the consumer sends an acknowledgement (ACK), which allows the broker to redeliver messages if a consumer fails before acknowledging.

questions.prompt: A RabbitMQ-based app must broadcast every message to all queues bound to an exchange, regardless of routing key. Which exchange type should be used?
choices: Direct
Headers
Fanout
Topic
questions.correctChoice: Fanout
questions.explanation: A fanout exchange copies messages to every bound queue. Direct routes on an exact routing key, topic on pattern matches, and headers on message header attributes.

questions.prompt: Which messaging protocol is described as a simple, text-based wire protocol that lets clients talk to almost any message broker?
choices: STOMP
OpenWire
Kafka Producer API
AMQP
questions.correctChoice: STOMP
questions.explanation: STOMP (Simple Text-Oriented Messaging Protocol) is a simple text-based protocol supported by Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ and works with many brokers and clients.

questions.prompt: Which protocol is a lightweight publish/subscribe protocol that uses minimal bandwidth and is common for IoT and machine-to-machine communication?
choices: SMTP
MQTT
STOMP
LDAP
questions.correctChoice: MQTT
questions.explanation: MQTT is a lightweight pub/sub protocol for constrained devices and M2M messaging, in which clients publish to or subscribe on topic names through a broker.

questions.prompt: An existing application uses RabbitMQ topic exchanges with routing key patterns and the AMQP protocol. The company wants a managed service but does not want to rewrite the application to use AWS-specific messaging APIs. What should it use?
choices: Amazon SNS with filter policies and SQS queues
Amazon MSK with a new Kafka consumer group
Amazon SQS FIFO queues with message group IDs
Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
questions.correctChoice: Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
questions.explanation: Amazon MQ keeps the broker's native protocol and routing features (exchanges, bindings, routing keys), so the application migrates without being rewritten. SNS and SQS offer similar patterns, but with different APIs.

questions.prompt: A legacy Java application communicates with its broker using JMS over the OpenWire protocol. It must move to AWS quickly, with minimal code changes and no self-managed brokers. Which option fits best?
choices: Amazon MQ for Apache ActiveMQ
Amazon SQS standard queues
Amazon SNS with an HTTP subscription
Amazon MQ for RabbitMQ
questions.correctChoice: Amazon MQ for Apache ActiveMQ
questions.explanation: OpenWire is an ActiveMQ protocol, and Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ lets JMS applications connect with minimal changes. SQS and SNS would need code changes.

questions.prompt: Which AWS service is a fully managed service for building and running applications that use Apache Kafka to process streaming data?
choices: Amazon AppFlow
Amazon MSK
Amazon MQ
Amazon SNS
questions.correctChoice: Amazon MSK
questions.explanation: Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK) runs Apache Kafka clusters for you so that Kafka applications can run on AWS without managing the Kafka infrastructure.

questions.prompt: In Apache Kafka, how are messages organised?
choices: Producers write to queues, with a visibility timeout on each message
Producers send to topics, and each consumer is pushed a copy
Producers write to topics, stored in partitions that consumers read from
Producers write to exchanges that route to queues by binding
questions.correctChoice: Producers write to topics, stored in partitions that consumers read from
questions.explanation: Kafka messages are organised into topics, whose data is stored in partitions on the cluster (which can span machines). Producers publish and consumers listen using the Kafka APIs.

questions.prompt: A team needs a high-volume event stream where several independent consumer applications can each read the same ordered stream, with data kept for later re-reading. Which service type suits this best?
choices: An SQS standard queue
An SNS standard topic with email subscribers
Apache Kafka on Amazon MSK
An SQS delay queue
questions.correctChoice: Apache Kafka on Amazon MSK
questions.explanation: Kafka retains data in partitioned topics that many consumers can read independently and replay. In SQS, consumers share a queue and a message is deleted once it is processed.

questions.prompt: In an Amazon MSK cluster running in ZooKeeper mode, which statement describes the node types?
choices: Brokers manage the cluster metadata, and ZooKeeper nodes store the messages
Brokers store and process messages, and ZooKeeper nodes manage metadata and coordination
Brokers run Kafka Connect, and ZooKeeper nodes expose SQS-compatible endpoints
Both node types store messages, but only ZooKeeper nodes accept producers
questions.correctChoice: Brokers store and process messages, and ZooKeeper nodes manage metadata and coordination
questions.explanation: Brokers handle storage and processing of messages. ZooKeeper tracks broker registration, topic configuration, cluster membership, quotas and ACLs.

questions.prompt: A startup has unpredictable Kafka traffic and does not want to size, monitor or scale broker instances. Which MSK cluster type fits best?
choices: MSK Serverless, which manages capacity automatically and bills for usage
MSK Provisioned, where the broker instances are sized and scaled manually
A Kafka cluster on EC2 instances that the team manages itself
MSK Provisioned with additional ZooKeeper nodes added
questions.correctChoice: MSK Serverless, which manages capacity automatically and bills for usage
questions.explanation: Serverless clusters manage instances automatically and bill for usage, whereas Provisioned clusters require choosing and managing broker instances.

questions.prompt: A Kafka client application in a different VPC cannot connect to a newly created MSK cluster. By default, where must connections to an MSK cluster originate?
choices: From any AWS account in the same Region
From the same Availability Zone as the cluster
From any host on the internet
From within the VPC where the cluster was launched
questions.correctChoice: From within the VPC where the cluster was launched
questions.explanation: MSK clusters are launched in your VPC, and by default connections must come from that VPC. Public access can be enabled on a cluster after launch, or private connectivity can be provided between networks.

questions.prompt: Partners outside AWS need to connect Kafka clients directly to an existing MSK cluster over the internet. Which statement is correct?
choices: Clients connect to the ZooKeeper connection string to get public access
Public access can only be chosen when the cluster is created, so build a new cluster
Enable public access on the cluster after launch, and use the public bootstrap broker string
MSK clusters can never be reached from outside of their VPC
questions.correctChoice: Enable public access on the cluster after launch, and use the public bootstrap broker string
questions.explanation: Access is VPC-only by default, but public access can be turned on after the cluster is launched. Clients then use the public bootstrap broker endpoints (for example, the public SASL/IAM string) to connect.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of an MSK bootstrap broker string?
choices: It is the key that is used to encrypt the cluster's data at rest
It gives Kafka clients broker endpoints to start connecting to the cluster
It lists the ZooKeeper nodes that clients must write to directly
It stores the messages that belong to a particular Kafka topic
questions.correctChoice: It gives Kafka clients broker endpoints to start connecting to the cluster
questions.explanation: Bootstrap brokers are broker endpoints that a client connects to first to discover the rest of the cluster. The number of endpoints depends on the AZs the cluster spans, and there are separate strings for private and public access.

questions.prompt: A team wants to continuously copy data from MSK topics into S3 for analytics and avoid writing and operating a custom consumer application. Which feature should they use?
choices: MSK Connect with a Kafka Connect S3 sink connector
A Lambda function polling the ZooKeeper ensemble
An SQS queue subscribed to the Kafka topic
An SNS topic with a Firehose subscription polling Kafka
questions.correctChoice: MSK Connect with a Kafka Connect S3 sink connector
questions.explanation: MSK Connect runs Kafka Connect connectors as a managed feature. You upload the plugin to S3, create a plugin in MSK Connect, then create a connector pointing to the cluster and the target system.

questions.prompt: Which sequence correctly describes how to set up MSK Connect?
choices: Upload the plugin to an SNS topic, then create a connector inside SQS
Create a connector first, then upload the plugin onto a ZooKeeper node
Create a queue, subscribe the connector to that queue, then download a plugin
Get the plugin, upload it to S3, create an MSK Connect plugin, then create a connector
questions.correctChoice: Get the plugin, upload it to S3, create an MSK Connect plugin, then create a connector
questions.explanation: MSK Connect uses the Kafka Connect framework. Plugins are stored in S3, registered as an MSK Connect plugin, and used by a connector that specifies configuration for the source or target system.

questions.prompt: A company runs Apache Kafka on premises with many existing producers and consumers using the Kafka APIs. It wants to move to AWS, with no application rewrite and less cluster maintenance. Which option is best?
choices: Amazon SNS, by rewriting the producers to use topics
Amazon MSK
Amazon SQS, by rewriting the applications to use queues
Amazon AppFlow, by creating a flow per Kafka topic
questions.correctChoice: Amazon MSK
questions.explanation: MSK is compatible with the open-source Kafka APIs, so existing clients can connect with minimal changes, while AWS manages the cluster infrastructure.

questions.prompt: In an MSK cluster that uses ZooKeeper mode, what does Apache ZooKeeper do for Kafka?
choices: It stores the message data that producers write into the topic partitions
It encrypts the messages as they travel between the producers and the brokers
It handles coordination and metadata, such as broker registration and topic configuration
It runs the connectors that move the data from the cluster into S3
questions.correctChoice: It handles coordination and metadata, such as broker registration and topic configuration
questions.explanation: ZooKeeper provides distributed coordination: broker registration, topic configuration, cluster membership, quotas and ACLs. The brokers store and serve the messages.

questions.prompt: A team wants events from an MSK topic to be filtered, enriched and sent on to a target such as a Step Functions state machine, with little custom code. Which integration supports this?
choices: Amazon EventBridge Pipes with MSK as the source
An SQS delay queue between brokers
AWS AppFlow with MSK as the destination
SNS Message Data Protection on the MSK topic
questions.correctChoice: Amazon EventBridge Pipes with MSK as the source
questions.explanation: MSK has direct integration with EventBridge Pipes, which can use an MSK topic as a source and optionally filter and enrich events before sending them to a target.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS?
choices: Both services require the consumers to poll for new messages
SNS stores messages until they are polled, while SQS pushes them to subscribers
Both services push each message to every consumer at the same moment
SNS pushes messages to subscribers, while SQS holds messages until consumers poll
questions.correctChoice: SNS pushes messages to subscribers, while SQS holds messages until consumers poll
questions.explanation: SNS is a push-based pub/sub service. SQS is a pull-based queue where consumers poll and delete messages.

questions.prompt: When an image is uploaded to S3, the system must run thumbnail generation, virus scanning and metadata indexing independently. Each task can fail and retry without affecting the others, and workloads vary. Which design is best?
choices: Run all three of the tasks in sequence inside one single Lambda function
Send the S3 event to an SNS topic, with one SQS queue and consumer per task
Send the S3 event to a single SQS queue that is read by all three of the tasks
Send the S3 event to an SQS delay queue that every one of the tasks polls
questions.correctChoice: Send the S3 event to an SNS topic, with one SQS queue and consumer per task
questions.explanation: SNS fanout to separate queues gives each task its own durable copy of the event, independent retries and independent scaling. A single shared queue would give each message to only one task.

questions.prompt: Which requirement most clearly points to Amazon SQS FIFO rather than Amazon MSK?
choices: A data pipeline needs streaming connectors to databases and to S3
Existing producers already use the Apache Kafka client libraries today
Strictly ordered work items, each handled once by one worker, then removed
Several independent applications must each re-read the same event history
questions.correctChoice: Strictly ordered work items, each handled once by one worker, then removed
questions.explanation: SQS FIFO is a queue for ordered work items that are consumed and deleted. Replay by multiple consumers, Kafka API compatibility and connector ecosystems are strengths of MSK.

questions.prompt: What range of message retention periods can be configured for an Amazon SQS queue?
choices: From 60 seconds up to 14 days
From 1 hour up to 7 days
From 1 second up to 12 hours
From 1 day up to 365 days
questions.correctChoice: From 60 seconds up to 14 days
questions.explanation: SQS retention can be set between 60 seconds and 14 days, with a default of 4 days. Messages not consumed by then are deleted. 12 hours is the maximum visibility timeout, not retention.

questions.prompt: A single alert must reach an operations email address, an on-call phone by SMS and a Lambda function. Which feature lets the publisher send it once?
choices: An SQS delay queue with a message timer for each consumer
An SQS queue that is polled by three different consumers
Three separate SQS FIFO queues, one for each destination
An SNS topic with an email, an SMS and a Lambda subscription
questions.correctChoice: An SNS topic with an email, an SMS and a Lambda subscription
questions.explanation: SNS topics deliver one published message to all of their subscriptions, formatting it for each protocol, so publishers need not know about subscriber protocols.

questions.prompt: Which encryption options are available for data at rest in an SQS queue?
choices: Encryption that is available only on FIFO queues and nowhere else
Encryption that is possible only through a dedicated CloudHSM cluster
Server-side encryption, with SQS-managed keys or with AWS KMS keys
Encryption that is not supported for any SQS queues at all
questions.correctChoice: Server-side encryption, with SQS-managed keys or with AWS KMS keys
questions.explanation: SQS supports server-side encryption using either SQS-managed keys or AWS KMS keys. KMS keys offer more control and auditing.

questions.prompt: An order API receives bursts ten times the normal rate. The order processing writes to a relational database that can only sustain the normal rate, and no order may be lost. Which design handles this with the least change?
choices: The API writes straight to the database and relies on clients retrying with longer waits
The API calls the processing service synchronously, and that service is scaled out for bursts
The API publishes to an SNS topic that has an HTTP subscription to the processing service
The API writes orders to an SQS queue, and a fixed consumer fleet drains it at a sustainable rate
questions.correctChoice: The API writes orders to an SQS queue, and a fixed consumer fleet drains it at a sustainable rate
questions.explanation: A queue absorbs bursts durably and lets consumers pull at a controlled rate (load levelling). Direct, synchronous and push designs pass the burst through to the database.

questions.prompt: An application publishes events with a numeric attribute severity from 1 to 5. Requirements: every event goes to an analytics SQS queue, events with severity 4 or above go to an on-call phone by SMS, and events with severity 3 or below go to an email digest address. The publisher must publish only once. Which design meets this?
choices: Three topics, where the application chooses a topic according to the event's severity
One topic with three subscriptions: queue unfiltered, SMS for severity 4 and up, email for 3 and below
One topic, where the publisher sends twice, once for the queue and once for SMS or email
One SQS queue that is read by an application which sends the SMS and the email itself
questions.correctChoice: One topic with three subscriptions: queue unfiltered, SMS for severity 4 and up, email for 3 and below
questions.explanation: Subscription filter policies with numeric range matching route messages per subscriber, and a subscription without a filter policy receives everything, so one publish serves all three.

questions.prompt: A checkout service calls an invoicing service synchronously over HTTP. When invoicing is slow or down, checkout fails and customers cannot buy. Invoices may be generated a few minutes later. What should the architect do?
choices: Have checkout put an invoice request on an SQS queue that the invoicing service consumes
Replace the HTTP call with a second synchronous call to a backup invoicing service
Have the invoicing service poll the checkout database every second
Increase the HTTP timeout and add instances to the checkout service
questions.correctChoice: Have checkout put an invoice request on an SQS queue that the invoicing service consumes
questions.explanation: Introducing a queue decouples the services: checkout succeeds as soon as the request is queued and invoicing processes it when able. Longer timeouts and backup synchronous calls keep the tight coupling.

questions.prompt: A system handles a very high rate of independent events and must be cost-effective and highly scalable. Occasional duplicate delivery is acceptable provided the effect of processing is not duplicated. Which design is best?
choices: An SNS FIFO topic that delivers every one of the events to a single subscriber
An Amazon MQ broker that is configured with one single active queue
An SQS standard queue, with consumers that record event IDs to skip repeats
An SQS FIFO queue where every event is sent using one single message group
questions.correctChoice: An SQS standard queue, with consumers that record event IDs to skip repeats
questions.explanation: Standard queues scale to very high throughput, and idempotent consumers make at-least-once delivery safe. A single FIFO message group would serialise everything and limit throughput.

questions.prompt: Messages in an SQS FIFO queue must become available to consumers 5 minutes after they are sent, and order must be kept. A developer proposes per-message timers. What is the correct approach?
choices: Use per-message timers, which FIFO queues fully support for this purpose
Raise the visibility timeout of the queue to 300 seconds for every message
Use long polling with a wait time of 300 seconds on the consumers
Set a queue-level delay of 300 seconds, as FIFO queues lack message timers
questions.correctChoice: Set a queue-level delay of 300 seconds, as FIFO queues lack message timers
questions.explanation: Per-message timers are not supported on FIFO queues, but the queue-level DelaySeconds (up to 15 minutes) applies to all messages and preserves order. Visibility timeout and long polling do not delay a new message.

questions.prompt: An SNS topic delivers to an SQS queue that is encrypted with the AWS managed key for SQS (alias/aws/sqs). Messages are not arriving in the queue. What is the correct fix?
choices: Encrypt the queue with a customer managed key whose key policy allows SNS
Disable the queue's access policy completely so that SNS is able to write
Increase the queue's retention period up to its maximum of 14 days
Switch the queue to FIFO and change the topic into a standard topic
questions.correctChoice: Encrypt the queue with a customer managed key whose key policy allows SNS
questions.explanation: The AWS managed key's policy cannot be edited to grant the SNS service access. A customer managed key lets you add a key policy statement allowing SNS to generate data keys and decrypt, so delivery to the encrypted queue works.

questions.prompt: Applications in Account A must send messages to an SQS queue in Account B, but must not be able to receive or delete messages. What is the best way to grant this?
choices: Share the queue's visibility timeout settings with Account A's principals
Add a queue policy statement allowing sqs:SendMessage for the Account A principal
Create IAM users in Account B and give their access keys to Account A
Give the Account A root user full SQS permissions inside Account B
questions.correctChoice: Add a queue policy statement allowing sqs:SendMessage for the Account A principal
questions.explanation: An SQS queue access policy is a resource-based policy that can grant specific actions, such as only SendMessage, to principals in other accounts. This is least privilege without sharing long-term credentials.
